_draft.source_quote: If the money in a bank account has dwindled from £1,000 to £1, only the remaining £1 is capable of being substituted by something else; the £999 has ceased to exist. This explains “the lowest intermediate balance” principle.
_draft.uncertainty: Durant (para 40) allows 'backwards tracing' where there is a coordinated transaction; the scenario expressly excludes any intention to replace, so the cap applies. The [2016] AC 297 report citation was not checked.

subject: Trusts
title: Dishonest assistance: the trustee's honesty is irrelevant (Royal Brunei Airlines v Tan)
scenario: Celia Osei, a trustee, honestly but wrongly believed that the trust deed allowed her to lend £150,000 of trust money to a property developer. She asked her accountant, Darius Webb, to arrange the transfer. Darius knew the loan was plainly outside the trustee's powers and knew that Celia mistakenly thought otherwise, but he said nothing and arranged the transfer. He received none of the trust money. The developer became insolvent and the money was lost. The beneficiaries sue Darius.
stem: Which of the following best describes Darius's liability?

options.A: He is not liable, because accessory liability requires a dishonest and fraudulent design on the part of the trustee, and Celia was honest.
options.B: He is not liable, because he received none of the trust property.
options.C: He is liable only if he was negligent, because the test is whether he ought to have known of the breach.
options.D: He is liable only if he himself regarded his conduct as dishonest by his own standards.
options.E: He is liable to make good the loss as a dishonest assistant, because he dishonestly assisted in the breach of trust; Celia's honesty does not matter.

explanation: In Royal Brunei Airlines v Tan the Privy Council held that dishonesty is both a necessary and a sufficient ingredient of accessory liability. A person who dishonestly procures or assists in a breach of trust is liable to make good the resulting loss, and it is not necessary that the trustee was also acting dishonestly. Lord Nicholls gave the example of a solicitor who knows that a trustee is mistakenly making a payment in plain breach of trust and dishonestly leaves him under that misapprehension. Dishonesty here means not acting as an honest person would in the circumstances. That is an objective standard, assessed in the light of what the defendant actually knew. Darius knew the loan was outside the trustee's powers and knew Celia was mistaken, yet he arranged the transfer without telling her. An honest person would not do that. He is liable for the £150,000 loss even though he received nothing.

why_wrong.A: Royal Brunei rejected any requirement that the trustee be dishonest; what matters is the accessory's state of mind.
why_wrong.B: Receipt is required for knowing receipt, not for accessory liability, which does not depend on receiving trust property.
why_wrong.C: Negligence is not enough; dishonesty is the touchstone of accessory liability.
why_wrong.D: The standard of honesty is objective; individuals cannot set their own standards.

key_rule: A person who dishonestly assists in a breach of trust is liable for the loss, whether or not the trustee was dishonest; dishonesty is judged objectively (Royal Brunei v Tan).
authority: Royal Brunei Airlines Sdn Bhd v Tan [1995] UKPC 4, [1995] 2 AC 378

_draft.spec_topic: Liability of strangers to the trust: dishonest assistance
_draft.source_quote: A liability in equity to make good resulting loss attaches to a person who dishonestly procures or assists in a breach of trust or fiduciary obligation. It is not necessary that, in addition the trustee or fiduciary was acting dishonestly
_draft.uncertainty: Later cases (Twinsectra; Barlow Clowes; Ivey v Genting) refined how dishonesty is assessed but do not affect this answer.

subject: Trusts
title: Knowing receipt: no liability for a bona fide purchaser who later learns of the breach
scenario: In breach of trust, Lionel Grant, the sole trustee of a family trust in England, sold 5,000 trust shares to Imogen Clarke for their full market value. Imogen acted in good faith and had no notice, actual or constructive, that the sale was a breach of trust. Eighteen months later a beneficiary tells Imogen about the breach. She still holds the shares. The beneficiaries claim that she is now personally liable in knowing receipt.
stem: Is Imogen liable in knowing receipt?

options.A: Yes, because she learned of the breach of trust while she still held the shares.
options.B: Yes, because liability for receiving trust property transferred in breach of trust is strict.
options.C: Yes, if the court considers it unconscionable for her to keep the shares now that she knows of the breach.
options.D: No, because as a bona fide purchaser for value without notice she took free of the beneficiaries' interest, and her later knowledge of the breach gives rise to no liability in knowing receipt.
options.E: No, but only because liability in knowing receipt requires the recipient to have acted dishonestly.

explanation: Knowing receipt is a personal liability that can arise where trust property is transferred in breach of trust to a recipient who, with the necessary knowledge, deals with it while the beneficiaries still have an equitable interest in it. In Byers v Saudi National Bank the Supreme Court held that the claim depends on the claimant retaining an equitable proprietary interest in the property when it reaches the defendant. Lord Briggs said it is clear that where trust property is transferred in breach of trust to equity's darling, a bona fide purchaser for value without notice, the transferee's later acquisition of knowledge of the breach gives rise to no liability in knowing receipt. Imogen paid full value in good faith without notice, so she took the shares free of the beneficiaries' interest. Learning of the breach eighteen months later cannot revive a claim against her. The beneficiaries' remedy lies against Lionel personally, and in tracing into the sale proceeds he received.

why_wrong.A: Later knowledge matters for a volunteer recipient, not for a bona fide purchaser who took free of the trust.
why_wrong.B: Knowing receipt is fault-based and in any case never reaches a bona fide purchaser for value without notice.
why_wrong.C: Whatever the knowledge test, once the interest is defeated by sale to equity's darling, no unconscionability inquiry arises.
why_wrong.E: Dishonesty is the test for dishonest assistance, not knowing receipt; Imogen escapes because she took free of the interest.

key_rule: Knowing receipt requires the beneficiaries' equitable interest to subsist when the property is received; a bona fide purchaser without notice who later learns of the breach is not liable.
authority: Byers v Saudi National Bank [2023] UKSC 51, [2024] AC 1191; BCCI (Overseas) Ltd v Akindele [2001] Ch 437

_draft.source_quote: it is I think clear that after such a transfer, the subsequent acquisition by the transferee D of knowledge that the transfer had involved a breach of trust by T gives rise to no liability in knowing receipt.
